The Ten Best History Books of 2025
Our favorite titles of the year resurrect overlooked histories and examine how the United States ended up where it is today
Meilan Solly
| Senior Associate Digital Editor, History
November 25, 2025
Share
Copy link Email SMS Facebook X Reddit LinkedIn Bluesky Print Add as preferred source
Smithsonian magazine's picks for the best history books of 2025 include We the People , The Stolen Crown and Medicine River .
Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz
Next July, the United States will mark the 250th anniversary of its founding, a milestone set to be celebrated across the country. American history will serve as the centerpiece of many of these events, with the semiquincentennial offering a chance to reflect on the nation’s triumphs and failures alike. But the question of which stories will be told—and how they’ll be framed—remains a point of contention .
This debate over how to tell American history is unfolding at a “moment that people have described as existential, certainly a moment of division ,” documentarian Ken Burns told Smithsonian magazine earlier this month, in a wide-ranging interview about his new American Revolution series on PBS. “Maybe there could be some understanding that during this revolutionary period, we were more divided than we are now. And maybe by going back and reinvesting some time in this origin story, we’ll be able to put the ‘us’ back in the U.S.”
Against this backdrop, the ten history books we’ve chosen to highlight this year serve a dual purpose. Some reflect on the fraught nature of the current moment, detailing how the nation’s past—including the American Revolution and the creation of the U.S. Constitution—informs its present and future. Others offer a respite from today’s reality, transporting readers to places like Tudor England and ancient Egypt. From a biography of Amelia Earhart to the story of the sinking of the Edmund Fitzgerald , these are ten of Smithsonian magazine’s favorite history books of 2025.
We the People: A History of the U.S. Constitution by Jill Lepore
Jill Lepore ’s 700-page history of the U.S. Constitution revolves around a central conceit: that this founding charter , written by a group of white men in Philadelphia 238 years ago , was never meant to be a static document. As Lepore, a historian at Harvard University and staff writer at the New Yorker , writes in We the People , “Through experiment and experience, Americans came to agree that if such a strange, fragile thing as a written constitution were to endure, it would, as time passed … need to be both revised and repaired, improved and updated.”
This argument runs counter to originalism , a theory that promotes interpretation of the Constitution as it was understood at the time it was written . In Lepore’s view, originalists “rely on an artificially bounded historical record that disadvantages the descendants of people” who had no say in the creation of the Constitution, including women, the enslaved and Native Americans. Legal scholars rely on the published writings of powerful men to debate the Constitution, she argues. But historians must consider the opinions of those who didn’t serve as delegates to the Constitutional Convention and had no way of publishing their opinions in 1787. “For the historian,” Lepore writes, “unpublished documents written by less powerful people do not ‘count for nothing,’” as former Solicitor General Robert Bork argued in 1990. “In fact,” she says, “they count for rather a lot.”
We the People builds on the Amendments Project , an initiative Lepore spearheaded that tracks more than 11,000 amendments proposed in Congress between 1789 and 2022. The vast majority of these efforts never came to fruition, with just 27 amendments ratified by the states since 1791. But that doesn’t mean the failed proposals are insignificant: As Lepore tells the Guardian , “It’s so hard to amend the Constitution. If you look at efforts to do it, you just see this really big, colorful canvas of contestation, which is narratively rich and politically important.” Written in lyrical prose, Lepore’s new book unpacks this history, presenting a timely argument about the need for the Constitution to keep evolving to meet society’s needs.
We the People: A History of the U.S. Constitution
Published to mark the 250th anniversary of the nation’s founding―the anniversary, too, of the first state constitutions― We the People offers a wholly new history of the Constitution.
Buy Now
The Stolen Crown: Treachery, Deceit and the Death of the Tudor Dynasty by Tracy Borman
From the beginning of Elizabeth I’s 44-year reign in 1558, a recurring question dominated domestic debates: Who would succeed the unmarried , childless Tudor queen—the last survivor of Henry VIII’s three children —if she died without naming an heir? In an era when cousins waged war over their competing claims to the English throne, securing the succession was of paramount importance. Yet Elizabeth continually demurred when pressed on the issue, fearing that her detractors would rally behind whomever she named as next in line.
Traditional lore suggests that Elizabeth only chose a successor on her deathbed in 1603, when she supposedly told advisers she would “ have none but him ”—a reference to James VI of Scotland, the son of her erstwhile rival and cousin, Mary, Queen of Scots .
But what if that lore had no basis in reality? That’s the provocative claim put forth by historian Tracy Borman in The Stolen Crown , a meticulously researched must-read for Tudor enthusiasts.
A lightsheet used to reveal hidden text in a manuscript of William Camden's Annals
© The British Library Board
“This scene has been replayed (and embellished) numerous times in the 400 or so years since Elizabeth’s death,” Borman writes. England and Scotland “had been fierce rivals for centuries [and] were now forged into an uncomfortably United Kingdom. And it had all begun with a lie.”
Borman based her thesis on new research into William Camden ’s Annals , the main historical source for the deathbed anecdote. In 2023, advanced imaging of handwritten manuscripts housed at the British Library showed that Camden censored his original draft to flatter James, whose patronage he relied on to publish the work, and make the king’s “accession appear more predetermined than it had been,” according to Borman.
Borman argues that the famous story was entirely invented, with Elizabeth never actually naming a successor, in part because she was so ill that she was unable to speak in her final days. While the queen had seemingly settled on James as her heir long before her death, taking steps to prepare him for the burdens of kingship via regular correspondence , she was unwilling to name him explicitly. “The real story of the Elizabethan succession,” Borman writes, “was altogether darker and more turbulent than Camden’s fiction.”
The Stolen Crown: Treachery, Deceit and the Death of the Tudor Dynasty
From an acclaimed royal historian, the dramatic and untold story of the lie about the controversial succession that ended the Tudor era and changed the course of British history
Buy Now
The Gales of November: The Untold Story of the Edmund Fitzgerald by John U. Bacon
Published 50 years after the sinking of the Edmund Fitzgerald , John U. Bacon ’s The Gales of November offers a definitive account of the famous maritime tragedy, which claimed the lives of 29 men on November 10, 1975. Drawing on books, documentaries, articles and hundreds of original interviews, Bacon—a journalist who previously profiled the Halifax explosion of 1917—weaves a vivid narrative that will satisfy both Fitzgerald experts and readers new to the disaster. As Christopher Wilson , a curator at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History , tells Smithsonian , “I’ve spent my life sailing, fishing and swimming in the Great Lakes. Each week, my family passed Detroit’s Mariners’ Church , which still holds a memorial [every November]. Even with that lifelong connection, I learned something new on every page of Bacon’s masterpiece.”
Bacon grew up in the Great Lakes region and had long been aware of the Fitzgerald . Instead of attempting to determine what led the ship to sink ( theories abound , but no definitive answer has emerged), the journalist wanted to shine a light on the freighter’s crew. “They were common men doing uncommon work, is how I describe it,” Bacon told Smithsonian magazine’s podcast, “ There’s More to That ,” earlier this month. “Blue-collar guys, blue-collar families, felt lucky to get out of World War II alive, felt lucky to get out of the mines and the factories and the farms. But it was a hard, hard life. They worked very hard. They’re very stoic. They enjoyed a good prank. They played a lot of cards. They drank a lot of beer. That’s the short profile.”
The Gales of November: The Untold Story of the Edmund Fitzgerald
On the 50th anniversary of the Edmund Fitzgerald ’s sinking, the bestselling author of The Great Halifax Explosion tells the definitive story of the “Mighty Fitz.”
Buy Now
The Trouble of Color: An American Family Memoir by Martha S. Jones
When Martha S. Jones enrolled in a Black studies class during her freshman year of college, she found that a fellow student often stared at her with “barely contained contempt,” as she recalls in The Trouble of Color . Tensions came to a head when Jones—now a historian at Johns Hopkins University—gave a presentation on the Black psychiatrist and philosopher Frantz Fanon . The classmate jumped to his feet before Jones had finished her talk, telling the professor, “Enough of this. We shouldn’t have to listen to this.” The implication was clear: Jones, the daughter of a white mother and a Black father, was “not enough,” she writes. “Not enough for Black studies, for Fanon, for our coursework. My very person—skin too light, hair too limp, features too pointed, diction too suburban—unsettled, perplexed and even provoked.”
This incident serves as the opening of Jones’ latest book, a memoir that examines the tenuous, ever-shifting nature of the color line. Drawing on photographs, letters, newspaper clippings, oral histories and more, The Trouble of Color traces the stories of Jones’ ancestors, from her grandfather David Dallas Jones , the president of a Black women’s college, to her earliest known relative, her great-great-great-grandmother Nancy Belle Graves . “Nancy bequeathed to us not only her portrait but also the trouble of color—somewhere between too little and too much of it,” Jones writes.
Unlike Jones’ previous scholarly studies , The Trouble of Color is a deeply personal narrative. Artfully blending genealogy, historical research and self-reflection, the book is both a testament to the importance of preserving Black history and a compelling account of a single family’s trials and successes. As Jones told Smithsonian in March, the first-person format enabled her “to fully enter the story of my family past: as a descendant, as a researcher and as a storyteller. My histories help readers arrive at how to think; this memoir invites readers to also reflect on how to feel.”
The Trouble of Color: An American Family Memoir
Journeying across centuries, from rural Kentucky and small-town North Carolina to New York City and its suburbs, The Trouble of Color is a lyrical, deeply felt meditation on the most fundamental matters of identity, belonging and family.

The Last Dynasty: Ancient Egypt From Alexander the Great to Cleopatra by Toby Wilkinson
Few ancients wield as much fascination for the public as Alexander the Great , the Macedonian king who conquered Egypt in the fourth century B.C.E., and Cleopatra , the last ruler of Egypt, who died in 30 B.C. E. In The Last Dynasty , Egyptologist Toby Wilkinson capitalizes on this interest to draw readers into a sweeping history that covers much more than the famous figures in its title, looking at those who lived and ruled in between them: the Ptolemies . For all of its name recognition, Ptolemaic Egypt is understudied, “thought of as too Egyptian for most classicists and too Greek for many Egyptologists,” in the words of Egyptologist Campbell Price . Wilkinson’s book aims to bridge that gap, recognizing the “unusual dynamism and creativity” of this overlooked era, he writes.
Based on a wide array of sources, including the writings of ancient historians like Strabo , lesser-known inscriptions on statues and steles , and thousands of papyrus documents , The Last Dynasty tells the story of a multicultural land “that cherished its ancient customs but also sought to reinterpret and reinvent them to suit the changing times,” as Wilkinson puts it. While kings and queens are prominent players in the book, Wilkinson’s greatest triumph is his evocation of the lives of everyday people in Ptolemaic Egypt, from Ptolemaois, a soldier who “not only had access to, but read and enjoyed, a pioneering study by one of the greatest scientific thinkers of the day,” to Pakhom, an Egyptian-born official who presided over construction of a local temple dedicated to Cleopatra.
The Last Dynasty: Ancient Egypt From Alexander the Great to Cleopatra
One of the world’s leading Egyptologists tells the rich and fascinating story of ancient Egypt’s last dynasty.
Buy Now
The Rembrandt Heist: The Story of a Criminal Genius, a Stolen Masterpiece and an Enigmatic Friendship by Anthony Amore
In 2015, Anthony Amore , director of security at Boston’s Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, arranged a meeting with an unlikely companion: Myles Connor, a man described by Boston magazine as “the world’s greatest art thief.” The pair had long known each other by reputation, but this encounter marked the first time they’d spoken directly. As the chief investigator tasked with recovering 13 artworks stolen from the Gardner Museum in 1990, Amore wanted to ask if Connor, who knew all of the heist’s potential suspects, could help him get the lost paintings back. In response, Connor suggested the perpetrator wanted “to know that they aren’t going to get in trouble for dealing with you.” Ultimately, the thief agreed with Amore, saying the missing works “belong back in the Gardner Museum.”
A decade later, Amore’s unlikely friendship with Connor hasn’t yielded an answer to the biggest unsolved art heist in modern history. But the relationship did provide the security expert and author with material for The Rembrandt Heist , his propulsive new account of Connor’s criminal career. Based on interviews with the art thief and his lifelong best friend, Al Dotoli , as well as police records, newspaper accounts and other sources, the book centers on Connor’s 1975 theft of a Rembrandt van Rijn painting housed at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. Connor and an associate simply purchased tickets, walked into the museum and took the canvas off the wall, striking a guard with a pistol when he tried to intervene.
A few months after the theft, Connor was arrested on unrelated art theft charges. In his absence, investigators focused their interest on Dotoli, unaware that he hadn’t been involved in the heist. Ultimately, Dotoli, with Connor’s blessing, cooperated with authorities to return the artwork—which, as it turned out, the art thief had only stolen in the first place to use as a bargaining chip . The risky ploy worked: In exchange for the safe recovery of the Rembrandt, authorities shaved 11 years off Connor’s 15-year prison sentence.
The Rembrandt Heist: The Story of a Criminal Genius, a Stolen Masterpiece and an Enigmatic Friendship
A true crime tale of unbelievable friendship, loyalty, criminal genius and a staggeringly audacious plot to steal one of the world’s most valuable paintings—and return it

Unabridged: The Thrill of (and Threat to) the Modern Dictionary by Stefan Fatsis
Stefan Fatsis ’ Unabridged is a charming celebration of lexicography , paying tribute to dictionaries and their creators even as the author acknowledges that the rapid pace of the internet threatens to render storied publishers like the Oxford English Dictionary obsolete. Drawing in large part on Fatsis’ own experiences at Merriam-Webster , where he spent several years as a self-described “lexicographer-in-training slash journalist-in-residence,” the book confronts “the demands of dictionary-making in the instant-gratification digital age.”
How, for example, does one decide when the word “ sheeple ” has gained enough cultural traction to justify a definition in the dictionary? And what real-world example should accompany this definition? Fatsis, who wrote the Merriam-Webster entry in question, selected a CNN review of an iPhone battery case that referred to Apple lovers as “sheeple”; the quotation sparked an online outcry and was later removed. Unabridged poses other timely questions, too: What criteria should be used to determine a dictionary’s word of the year ? How soon should a dictionary of record add a definition for a rapidly evolving phenomenon like Covid-19 ? The answer, in Merriam-Webster’s case, was “just 34 days since the lexical item Covid-19 was coined,” according to Unabridged .
Part history of the dictionary-making business and part analysis of the contemporary lexicography industry, Unabridged is ultimately a love letter to “a quirky and charming subculture of word-lovers and obsessives,” a story, Fatsis writes, “about language and its power to shape us, to influence us, to annoy and rouse us—to be preserved for eternity by a concept more than four millennia old .”
Unabridged: The Thrill of (and Threat to) the Modern Dictionary
A vibrant, lively and illuminating journey through the exotic world of Merriam-Webster, dictionaries and language, at a time of rapid-fire change in the way we create, consume, define and use words
Buy Now
Medicine River: A Story of Survival and the Legacy of Indian Boarding Schools by Mary Annette Pember
Between 1819 and 1969, at least 973 Native American children died while attending Indian boarding schools in the U.S., where hundreds of thousands of youths were forced to live apart from their families and assimilate into white society. The true number of fatalities caused by these institutions’ repressive—and often abusive —conditions is likely significantly higher.
In the introduction to Medicine River , an account of the generational toll inflicted by these institutions, Mary Annette Pember deftly summarizes the schools’ legacy: “Because it was framed as a humane alternative to outright extermination, little thought was given to the generational fallout and trauma ignited by these policies,” the Ojibwe journalist writes. “Quite simply: Boarding schools were intended to destroy Indian families in order to destroy tribes to free up land for white settlement and exploitation.”
Pember’s incisive, heart-wrenching book is grounded in the experiences of her mother, Bernice Rabideaux , who was 5 years old when she and her siblings were separated from their parents and sent to a Catholic school on Wisconsin’s Bad River Reservation. The nuns instilled a message in Rabideaux’s mind: that Native Americans were “dirty, savage, backward, uncivilized,” according to Medicine River . This sentiment “took root in her behaviors, too,” leading her to fill her children’s days “with constant cleaning and scrubbing.” As Pember recalls, “Creating our family was part of her master plan to reinvent herself, to become worthy of respect. To become white. In many ways, she achieved her goal, but at the same time, the scheme choked her.”
It was only after Rabideaux’s death in 2011 that Pember decided to investigate her mother’s past in depth, connecting anecdotes to written records and other archival materials. The initial discoveries the journalist made pushed her to begin a project whose scope went far beyond her own family. Medicine River “is, I suppose, above all, a quest,” she writes. “To understand myself, our family’s collective disease, Indian people’s unparalleled ability to survive and the history of Indian boarding schools.”
Medicine River: A Story of Survival and the Legacy of Indian Boarding Schools
A sweeping and deeply personal account of Native American boarding schools in the United States, and the legacy of abuse wrought by them in an attempt to destroy Native culture and life
Buy Now
The Aviator and the Showman: Amelia Earhart, George Putnam and the Marriage That Made an American Icon by Laurie Gwen Shapiro
Amelia Earhart is one of the most famous women in American history. Yet she’s shrouded in misconceptions “about her personality, her career, her goals, her sexuality” and, of course, her disappearance in 1937, writes journalist Laurie Gwen Shapiro in The Aviator and the Showman , a breezy biography that seeks to set the record straight. Earhart , in Shapiro’s view, was a more complex figure than often acknowledged, a woman who was “ambitious, courageous, intelligent, curious, sexual, overconfident, lazy, kindhearted, shrewd and flawed.”
Earhart’s airbrushed legacy, The Aviator and the Showman argues, is largely the creation of her husband, George P. Putnam , a roguish showman whom Shapiro describes as “the publishing world’s P.T. Barnum .” After organizing a promotional competition that allowed an unseasoned Boy Scout to accompany an expedition to Antarctica , Putnam shifted his efforts to creating a female counterpart to Charles Lindbergh , whose memoir he’d published in 1927.
Quickly transitioning from Earhart’s book publisher to her romantic partner, Putnam devised increasingly dangerous publicity schemes that culminated in the aviator’s fatal attempt to fly around the world. But he isn’t entirely to blame for Earhart’s death, Shapiro argues: The trailblazing pilot was highly ambitious herself, and “she recognized in [Putnam] a strategic ally who could propel her stalled magnificent career ambitions forward and provide an escape from financial instability.” The author adds, “Despite a final catastrophe of their own making, their daring ventures propelled aviation forward and laid a lasting foundation, inspiring generations to pursue their dreams against formidable odds and empowering women worldwide.”
The Aviator and the Showman: Amelia Earhart, George Putnam and the Marriage That Made an American Icon
The riveting and cinematic story of a partnership that would change the world forever
Buy Now
The Fate of the Day: The War for America, Fort Ticonderoga to Charleston, 1777-1780 by Rick Atkinson
In 2019, Rick Atkinson published The British Are Coming , the first entry in his magisterial trilogy about the American Revolution. Covering the first 21 months of the conflict, the author and historian’s opener received rave reviews for its humanization of a vast cast of characters. Now, with his second book in the series, The Fate of the Day , Atkinson repeats this achievement by vividly introducing readers to lesser-known figures such as Frederica Charlotte Louise Riedesel , a German baroness whose husband commanded Hessian troops, while also offering new perspectives on giants of the Revolution like George Washington and Benedict Arnold .
Ostensibly a work of military history focused on the war’s middle years, 1777 to 1780, The Fate of the Day reads more like a novel, capturing readers’ attention over more than 800 pages. Atkinson’s research skills and his ability to extract compelling details that bring centuries-old stories to life make this book a timely and necessary read, especially as the U.S. prepares to celebrate its 250th anniversary in 2026.
By 1777, “American ambitions had changed markedly since Lexington and Concord, from a demand to be fully British in rights and privileges to not being British at all but, rather, a free, independent people,” Atkinson writes in The Fate of the Day . “What form this new entity should take was still uncertain, as seen in the many metaphors used to describe the United States: a flight of birds, a flock of sheep, a swarm of fish or, as depicted on the Continental $6 bill, a beaver gnawing down a large tree. … Whatever the nation would become, the army must be the transformational agent in the ascent from colonial backwater to sovereign power.”
The Fate of the Day: The War for America, Fort Ticonderoga to Charleston, 1777-1780
Atkinson’s brilliant account of the lethal conflict between the Americans and the British offers not only deeply researched and spectacularly dramatic history, but also a new perspective on the demands that a democracy makes on its citizens.
